groups.name: Switching Concepts, VLANs, and InterVLAN Routing

questions.question: Which tasks can be accomplished by using the command history feature? (Choose two.)

options.text: View a list of commands entered in a previous session.
Recall up to 15 command lines by default.
Set the command history buffer size.
Save command lines in a log file for future reference.

questions.original: The history command allows you to view and reuse previously entered commands stored in the buffer. It is also used to manage the of the buffer.

explain.s: The command history keeps the commands you recently typed in a buffer, so you can **recall** them with the Up arrow (or Ctrl+P) instead of retyping. The buffer holds **10** lines by default, and you can **change its size**.
x: The buffer is cleared when you log out, so commands from a previous session are gone.
The default is 10 lines, not 15.
History stays in memory; it is not written to a log file.

questions.question: What is the first action in the boot sequence when a switch is powered on?

options.text: load the default Cisco IOS software

questions.original: The first action to take place when a switch is powered on is the POST or power-on self-test. POST performs tests on the CPU, memory, and flash in preparation for loading the boot loader.

explain.s: Power on → the switch first runs **POST** (power-on self-test), which checks the CPU, DRAM and flash. Only after POST passes does it load the boot loader.
x: Boot loader, CPU initialization and loading IOS all come after POST.

questions.question: What must an administrator have in order to reset a lost password on a router?
questions.original: Console access to the device through a terminal or terminal emulator software on a PC is required for password recovery.

explain.s: Password recovery needs **physical (console) access**: you connect to the console port, interrupt the boot, and bypass the startup configuration. It cannot be done remotely.

questions.question: When configuring a switch for SSH access, what other command that is associated with the login local command is required to be entered on the switch?

options.text: login block-for seconds attempts number within*seconds*

questions.original: The login local command designates that the local username database is used to authenticate interfaces such as console or vty.

explain.s: `login local` tells a line (console or VTY) to check the **local username database**. That database must have at least one entry, so you also need `username ... secret ...`.

questions.question: Which command displays information about the auto-MDIX setting for a specific interface?​
questions.original: To examine the auto-MDIX setting for a specific interface, the show controllers ethernet-controller command with the phy keyword should be used.

explain.s: Use **show controllers** to see the auto-MDIX setting of a specific interface (the full form includes the PHY keyword).
code: Switch# show controllers ethernet-controller fa0/1 phy
x: show interfaces shows status, errors and counters, not the MDIX setting.

questions.question: If one end of an Ethernet connection is configured for full duplex and the other end of the connection is configured for half duplex, where would late collisions be observed?

options.text: on both ends of the connection
on the full-duplex end of the connection
on the half-duplex end of the connection

questions.original: Full-duplex communications do not produce collisions. However, collisions often occur in half-duplex operations. When a connection has two different duplex configurations, the half-duplex end will experience late collisions. Collisions are found on Ethernet networks. Serial interfaces use technologies other than Ethernet.

explain.s: In a duplex mismatch, the **full-duplex** side transmits whenever it wants, so the **half-duplex** side keeps detecting collisions after it has already started sending. These are **late collisions**, and they show up on the half-duplex end.
x: Full-duplex ports do not use CSMA/CD, so they never count collisions.
Serial interfaces are not Ethernet.

questions.question: Which command is used to set the BOOT environment variable that defines where to find the IOS image file on a switch?
questions.original: The boot system command is used to set the BOOT environment variable. The config-register and confreg commands are used to set the configuration register. The boot loader command supports commands to format the flash file system, reinstall the operating system software, and recover from a lost or forgotten password.

explain.s: The **BOOT environment variable** says where the IOS image is. You set it with `boot system`.
x: config-register and confreg set the configuration register (a router feature), not the image path.

questions.question: What does a switch use to locate and load the IOS image?
questions.original: The BOOT environment variable contains the information about where to find the IOS image file.

explain.s: The boot loader reads the **BOOT environment variable** to find and load the IOS image. If the variable is not set, it searches flash for the first usable image.

questions.question: Which protocol adds security to remote connections?
questions.original: SSH allows a technician to securely connect to a remote network device for monitoring and troubleshooting. HTTP establishes web page requests. FTP manages file transfer. NetBEUI is not routed on the Internet. POP downloads email messages from email servers.

explain.s: **SSH** encrypts the whole remote session, including passwords. That makes it the secure replacement for Telnet.
x: FTP, HTTP and POP send data in plain text.
NetBEUI is an old, non-routable LAN protocol.

questions.question: What is a characteristic of an IPv4 loopback interface on a Cisco IOS router?​

options.text: The no shutdown command is required to place this interface in an UP state.​
It is a logical interface internal to the router.
Only one loopback interface can be enabled on a router.​
It is assigned to a physical port and can be connected to other devices.

questions.original: The loopback interface is a logical interface internal to the router and is automatically placed in an UP state, as long as the router is functioning. It is not assigned to a physical port and can therefore never be connected to any other device. Multiple loopback interfaces can be enabled on a router.

explain.s: A loopback is a **logical (software) interface inside the router**. It is up as long as the router is running and has no physical port.
x: It needs no `no shutdown`.
You can create many loopbacks.
It cannot be cabled to another device.

questions.question: What is the minimum Ethernet frame size that will not be discarded by the receiver as a runt frame?
questions.original: The minimum Ethernet frame size is 64 bytes. Frames smaller than 64 bytes are considered collision fragments or runt frames and are discarded.

explain.s: The minimum valid Ethernet frame is **64 bytes**. Anything smaller is a **runt** (usually a collision fragment) and is dropped. The maximum standard frame is 1518 bytes, which carries 1500 bytes of data.

questions.question: After which step of the switch bootup sequence is the boot loader executed?
questions.original:
The correct bootup sequence order is as follows:
1.- The switch loads and executes the POST.
2.- The switch loads the boot loader software.
3.- The boot loader performs low-level CPU initialization.
4.- The boot loader initializes the flash memory.
5.- The boot loader locates and loads the default IOS image.

explain.s: Boot order: 1) **POST**, 2) load the **boot loader**, 3) low-level CPU initialization, 4) initialize the flash file system, 5) load IOS. So the boot loader runs right **after POST**.

questions.question: Which impact does adding a Layer 2 switch have on a network?

options.text: an increase in the number of dropped frames
an increase in the size of the broadcast domain
an increase in the number of network collisions
an increase in the size of the collision domain

questions.original: Adding a Layer 2 switch to a network increases the number of collision domains and increases the size of the broadcast domain. Layer 2 switches do not decrease the amount of broadcast traffic, do not increase the amount of network collisions and do not increase the number of dropped frames.

explain.s: A Layer 2 switch forwards broadcasts out every port, so adding one makes the **broadcast domain bigger**. At the same time, each switch port is its own collision domain, so collision domains get *smaller* and more numerous.
x: Switches reduce collisions; they don't add them.
Collision domains shrink; they don't grow.

questions.question: Which characteristic describes cut-through switching?

options.text: Error-free fragments are forwarded, so switching occurs with lower latency.
Frames are forwarded without any error checking.
Only outgoing frames are checked for errors.
Buffering is used to support different Ethernet speeds.

questions.original: Cut-through switching reduces latency by forwarding frames as soon as the destination MAC address and the corresponding switch port are read from the MAC address table. This switching method does not perform any error checking and does not use buffers to support different Ethernet speeds. Error checking and buffers are characteristics of store-and-forward switching.

explain.s: **Cut-through** switching starts forwarding as soon as it has read the destination MAC address. It never checks the FCS, so frames are forwarded **without error checking**. That gives low latency.
x: Fragment-free is the variant that checks the first 64 bytes.
Buffering for mixed speeds is a store-and-forward feature.

questions.question: What is the significant difference between a hub and a Layer 2 LAN switch?

options.text: A hub extends a collision domain, and a switch divides collision domains.
A hub divides collision domains, and a switch divides broadcast domains.
Each port of a hub is a collision domain, and each port of a switch is a broadcast domain.
A hub forwards frames, and a switch forwards only packets.

questions.original: Hubs operate only at the physical layer, forwarding bits as wire signals out all ports, and extend the collision domain of a network. Switches forward frames at the data link layer and each switch port is a separate collision domain which creates more, but smaller, collision domains. Switches do not manage broadcast domains because broadcast frames are always forwarded out all active ports.

explain.s: A **hub** repeats bits out every port, so everything attached shares **one collision domain**. A **switch** makes **each port its own collision domain**. Both still forward broadcasts everywhere, so neither one splits broadcast domains.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about Ethernet switch frame forwarding decisions?

options.text: Frame forwarding decisions are based on MAC address and port mappings in the CAM table.
Cut-through frame forwarding ensures that invalid frames are always dropped.
Only frames with a broadcast destination address are forwarded out all active switch ports.
Unicast frames are always forwarded regardless of the destination MAC address.

questions.original: Cut-through frame forwarding reads up to only the first 22 bytes of a frame, which excludes the frame check sequence and thus invalid frames may be forwarded. In addition to broadcast frames, frames with a destination MAC address that is not in the CAM are also flooded out all active ports. Unicast frames are not always forwarded. Received frames with a destination MAC address that is associated with the switch port on which it is received are not forwarded because the destination exists on the network segment connected to that port.

explain.s: A switch forwards a frame by looking up the **destination MAC address in its MAC (CAM) table**, which maps MAC addresses to ports.
x: Cut-through can forward bad frames, because it does not check the FCS.
Unknown unicasts are flooded too, not just broadcasts.
A frame is filtered (dropped) if its destination is on the same port it arrived on.

questions.question: How do switch buffers affect network performance?

options.text: They provide error checking on the data received.
They store frames received, thus preventing premature frame discarding when network congestion occurs.
They provide extra memory for a particular port if autonegotiation of speed or duplex fails.
They hold data temporarily when a collision occurs until normal data transmission resumes.

questions.original: Switches have large frame buffers that allow data waiting to be transmitted to be stored so the data will not be dropped. This feature is beneficial especially if the incoming traffic is from a faster port than the egress port used for transmitting.

explain.s: Buffers **store frames temporarily** when a port is busy, for example when traffic from a fast port has to leave through a slower one. This stops frames from being dropped during congestion.

questions.question: Which switch characteristic helps keep traffic local and alleviates network congestion?
questions.original: Switches that have a lot of ports (high port density) reduce the number of switches required and keep some of the traffic locally on the switch, thus removing the need to send it between switches.

explain.s: **High port density** means more devices connect to the same switch. More traffic stays local instead of crossing uplinks between switches, which relieves congestion.

questions.question: Which switch component reduces the amount of packet handling time inside the switch?
questions.original: Application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) are used in Cisco switches to speed up switch operations so that the switch can have an increased number of ports without degrading switch performance.

explain.s: **ASICs** (application-specific integrated circuits) do the forwarding in hardware. That cuts the time each frame spends inside the switch.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. A switch receives a Layer 2 frame that contains a source MAC address of 000b.a023.c501 and a destination MAC address of 0050.0fae.75aa. Place the switch steps in the order they occur. (Not all options are used.)
questions.original: The first step a switch does when processing a frame is to see if the source MAC address is in the MAC address table. If the address is not there, the switch adds it. The switch then examines the destination MAC address and compares it to the MAC address table. If the address is in the table, the switch forwards the frame out the corresponding port. If the address is missing from the table, the switch will forward the frame to all ports except the port through which the frame arrived.

explain.s: Frame processing order: 1) Check whether the **source MAC** is in the table, and add it with the incoming port if it isn't. 2) Look up the **destination MAC**. 3) If it is known, forward out that port; if it is unknown, **flood** it out every port except the one it arrived on.

questions.question: What information is added to the switch table from incoming frames?

options.text: source MAC address and incoming port number
destination MAC address and incoming port number
source IP address and incoming port number
destination IP address and incoming port number

questions.original: A switch "learns" or builds the MAC address table based on the source MAC address as a frame comes into the switch. A switch forwards the frame onward based on the destination MAC address.

explain.s: Switches **learn** by recording the **source MAC address and the port the frame came in on**. They use the *destination* MAC only to decide where to forward the frame.
x: Layer 2 switches do not look at IP addresses when building the MAC table.

questions.question: Which switching method ensures that the incoming frame is error-free before forwarding?
questions.original: Two methods used by switches to transmit frames are store-and-forward and cut-through switching. The store-and-forward method performs error checking on the frame using the frame check sequence (FCS) value before sending the frame. In contrast, cut-through switching sends the frame as soon as the destination MAC address part of the header has been read and processed.

explain.s: **Store-and-forward** receives the whole frame and checks its **FCS (CRC)**. Only error-free frames are forwarded.
x: Cut-through does no error checking; fragment-free checks only the first 64 bytes.
FCS is a field in the frame, not a switching method.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. How many broadcast domains are displayed?
questions.original: A router defines a broadcast boundary, so every link between two routers is a broadcast domain. In the exhibit, 4 links between routers make 4 broadcast domains. Also, each LAN that is connected to a router is a broadcast domain. The 4 LANs in the exhibit result in 4 more broadcast domains, so there are 8 broadcast domains in all.

explain.s: Routers stop broadcasts, so **every router interface is the edge of a broadcast domain**. In the exhibit there are 4 LANs plus 4 router-to-router links: **4 + 4 = 8** broadcast domains.

questions.question: Under which two occasions should an administrator disable DTP while managing a local area network? (Choose two.)

options.text: when connecting a Cisco switch to a non-Cisco switch
when a neighbor switch uses a DTP mode of dynamic auto
when a neighbor switch uses a DTP mode of dynamic desirable
on links that should not be trunking
on links that should dynamically attempt trunking

questions.original: Cisco best practice recommends disabling DTP on links where trunking is not intended and when a Cisco switch is connected to a non-Cisco switch. DTP is required for dynamic trunk negotiation.

explain.s: Turn DTP off (`switchport nonegotiate`, with a manual trunk or access mode) on **links that should never trunk** and on **links to non-Cisco switches**, because DTP is Cisco-proprietary.

questions.question: Which two characteristics describe the native VLAN? (Choose two.)

options.text: Designed to carry traffic that is generated by users, this type of VLAN is also known as the default VLAN.
The native VLAN traffic will be untagged across the trunk link.
This VLAN is necessary for remote management of a switch.
High priority traffic, such as voice traffic, uses the native VLAN.
The native VLAN provides a common identifier to both ends of a trunk.

questions.original: The native VLAN is assigned to 802.1Q trunks to provide a common identifier to both ends of the trunk link. Whatever VLAN native number is assigned to a port, or if the port is the default VLAN of 1, the port does not tag any frame in that VLAN as the traffic travels across the trunk. At the other end of the link, the receiving device that sees no tag knows the specific VLAN number because the receiving device must have the exact native VLAN number. The native VLAN should be an unused VLAN that is distinct from VLAN1, the default VLAN, as well as other VLANs. Data VLANs, also known as user VLANs, are configured to carry user-generated traffic, with the exception of high priority traffic, such as VoIP. Voice VLANs are configured for VoIP traffic. The management VLAN is configured to provide access to the management capabilities of a switch.

explain.s: On an 802.1Q trunk, frames in the **native VLAN are sent untagged**. Both ends must agree on the same native VLAN, so it acts as a **common identifier** for that untagged traffic. Best practice is to use an unused VLAN for it, not VLAN 1.
x: User traffic belongs in data VLANs, and voice in the voice VLAN.
Remote management uses the management VLAN.

questions.question: On a switch that is configured with multiple VLANs, which command will remove only VLAN 100 from the switch?

options.text: Switch(config-if)# no switchport trunk allowed vlan 100

questions.original: To remove all VLANs from a switch, the delete flash:vlan.dat command would be used. To change the assigned VLAN for an interface, the no switchport access vlan 100 interface configuration command would be used. To remove VLAN 100 as an allowed VLAN on a trunk, the no switchport trunk allowed vlan 100 would be used, but this would not remove the VLAN from the switch. To delete a single VLAN, such as VLAN 100, the no vlan 100 global configuration command would be used.

explain.s: `no vlan 100` in global configuration mode deletes just that one VLAN.
x: `delete flash:vlan.dat` wipes **all** VLANs.
The two interface commands only change port membership; VLAN 100 still exists.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. A network administrator is reviewing port and VLAN assignments on switch S2 and notices that interfaces Gi0/1 and Gi0/2 are not included in the output. Why would the interfaces be missing from the output?

options.text: There is a native VLAN mismatch between the switches.
There is no media connected to the interfaces.
They are configured as trunk interfaces.

questions.original: Interfaces that are configured as trunks do not belong to a VLAN and therefore will not show in the output of the show vlan brief commands.

explain.s: `show vlan brief` lists only **access ports**. **Trunk ports** don't belong to a single VLAN, so they are left out. Use `show interfaces trunk` to see them.

questions.question: A network contains multiple VLANs spanning multiple switches. What happens when a device in VLAN 20 sends a broadcast Ethernet frame?

options.text: All devices in all VLANs see the frame.
Devices in VLAN 20 and the management VLAN see the frame.
Only devices in VLAN 20 see the frame.
Only devices that are connected to the local switch see the frame.

questions.original: VLANs create logical broadcast domains that can span multiple VLAN segments. Ethernet frames that are sent by a device on a specific VLAN can only be seen by other devices in the same VLAN.

explain.s: A VLAN is a **broadcast domain**. A broadcast from VLAN 20 reaches **only VLAN 20 devices**, even across trunks to other switches.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. All workstations are configured correctly in VLAN 20. Workstations that are connected to switch SW1 are not able to send traffic to workstations on SW2. What could be done to remedy the problem?

options.text: Allow VLAN 20 on the trunk link.
Enable DTP on both ends of the trunk.
Configure all workstations on SW1 to be part of the default VLAN.
Configure all workstations on SW2 to be part of the native VLAN.

questions.original: Enabling DTP on both switches simply allows negotiation of trunking. The "Negotiation of Trunking" line in the graphic shows that DTP is already enabled. The graphic also shows how the native VLAN is 1, and the default VLAN for any Cisco switch is 1. The graphic shows the PCs are to be in VLAN 20.

explain.s: The exhibit shows that VLAN 20 isn't in the trunk's allowed list, so VLAN 20 frames never cross it. Add it to the allowed list.
code: SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20
x: DTP is already negotiating, so enabling it changes nothing.
Moving the PCs to the default or native VLAN breaks the intended design.

questions.question: What happens to switch ports after the VLAN to which they are assigned is deleted?

options.text: The ports are placed in trunk mode.
The ports are assigned to VLAN1, the default VLAN.
The ports stop communicating with the attached devices.

questions.original: Any ports that are not moved to an active VLAN cannot communicate with other hosts after the VLAN is deleted. They must be assigned to an active VLAN or their VLAN must be created.

explain.s: When a VLAN is deleted, its ports **stay assigned to the missing VLAN** and become **inactive**. They can't communicate until you recreate the VLAN or assign the ports to another one. They do **not** fall back to VLAN 1.

questions.question: Match the IEEE 802.1Q standard VLAN tag field with the description. (Not all options are used.)
questions.original:
The IEEE 802.1Q standard header includes a 4-byte VLAN tag:
Type - A 2-byte value called the tag protocol ID (TPID) value.
User priority - A 3-bit value that supports level or service implementation.
Canonical Format Identifier (CFI) - A 1-bit identifier that enables Token Ring frames to be carried across Ethernet links.
VLAN ID (VID) - A 12-bit VLAN identification number that supports up to 4096 VLAN IDs.

explain.s:
The 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes:
**Type (TPID)** – 2 bytes, value 0x8100, marks the frame as tagged.
**User priority (PCP)** – 3 bits for CoS/QoS.
**CFI** – 1 bit (originally for Token Ring).
**VLAN ID (VID)** – 12 bits, so up to 4096 IDs.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. In what switch mode should port G0/1 be assigned if Cisco best practices are being used?
questions.original: The router is used to route between the two VLANs, thus switch port G0/1 needs to be configured in trunk mode.

explain.s: The router has to route between several VLANs over one link (router-on-a-stick), so the switch port facing it must be a **trunk**.

questions.question: Match the DTP mode with its function. (Not all options are used.)
questions.original: The dynamic auto mode makes the interface become a trunk interface if the neighboring interface is set to trunk or desirable mode. The dynamic desirable mode makes the interface actively attempt to convert the link to a trunk link. The trunk mode puts the interface into permanent trunking mode and negotiates to convert the neighboring link into a trunk link. The nonegotiate mode prevents the interface from generating DTP frames.

explain.s:
DTP modes:
**dynamic auto** – becomes a trunk only if the neighbor is trunk or desirable (passive).
**dynamic desirable** – actively asks to become a trunk.
**trunk** – always a trunk, and still sends DTP.
**nonegotiate** – stops sending DTP frames.

questions.question: Port Fa0/11 on a switch is assigned to VLAN 30. If the command no switchport access vlan 30 is entered on the Fa0/11 interface, what will happen?

options.text: An error message would be displayed.
Port Fa0/11 will be returned to VLAN 1.

questions.original: When the no switchport access vlan command is entered, the port is returned to the default VLAN 1. The port will remain active as a member of VLAN 1, and VLAN 30 will still be intact, even if no other ports are associated with it.

explain.s: Removing the access VLAN sends the port **back to VLAN 1** (the default). VLAN 30 itself is not deleted, and the port stays up.

questions.question: Which command displays the encapsulation type, the voice VLAN ID, and the access mode VLAN for the Fa0/1 interface?
questions.original:
The show interfaces switchport command displays the following information for a given port:
Switchport
Administrative Mode
Operational Mode
Administrative Trunking Encapsulation
Operational Trunking Encapsulation
Negotiation of Trunking
Access Mode VLAN
Trunking Native Mode VLAN
Administrative Native VLAN tagging
Voice VLAN

explain.s: `show interfaces <id> switchport` shows a port's VLAN settings: administrative and operational mode, trunk encapsulation, access VLAN, native VLAN and voice VLAN.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. A technician is programming switch SW3 to manage voice and data traffic through port Fa0/20. What, if anything, is wrong with the configuration?

options.text: There is nothing wrong with the configuration.
Interface Fa0/20 can only have one VLAN assigned.
The mls qos trust cos command should reference VLAN 35.
The command used to assign the voice VLAN to the switch port is incorrect.

questions.original: The voice VLAN should be configured with the switchport voice vlan 150 command. A switch interface can be configured to support one data VLAN and one voice VLAN. The mls qos trust cos associates with the interface. Voice traffic must be trusted so that fields within the voice packet can be used to classify it for QoS.

explain.s: A voice VLAN is assigned with **switchport voice vlan**, not switchport access vlan. A port can have one access (data) VLAN **and** one voice VLAN.

questions.question: Which four steps are needed to configure a voice VLAN on a switch port? (Choose four).

options.text: Configure the interface as an IEEE 802.1Q trunk.
Assign the voice VLAN to the switch port.
Activate spanning-tree PortFast on the interface.
Ensure that voice traffic is trusted and tagged with a CoS priority value.
Configure the switch port interface with subinterfaces.
Assign a data VLAN to the switch port.
Configure the switch port in access mode.

questions.original:
To add an IP phone, the following commands should be added to the switch port:
SW3(config-vlan)# vlan 150
SW3(config-vlan)# name voice
SW3(config-vlan)# int fa0/20
SW3(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW3(config-if)# mls qos trust cos
SW3(config-if)# switchport access vlan 150

explain.s: Voice VLAN setup: **create the voice VLAN**, put the port in **access mode**, **trust the CoS** marking from the phone, and **assign the voice VLAN** to the port.
x: The phone port is an access port, not a trunk, and no subinterfaces are needed.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. PC1 is unable to communicate with server 1. The network administrator issues the show interfaces trunk command to begin troubleshooting. What conclusion can be made based on the output of this command?

options.text: Interface G0/2 is not configured as a trunk.
The encapsulation on interface G0/1 is incorrect.
The DTP mode is incorrectly set to dynamic auto on interface G0/1.

questions.original: In the show interfaces trunk output, the G0/2 interface of DLS1 is not listed. This indicates the interface has probably not been configured as a trunk link. In the show interfaces trunk output, the G0/2 interface of DLS1 is not listed. This indicates the interface has probably not been configured as a trunk link.

explain.s: `show interfaces trunk` lists only interfaces that are trunking. **G0/2 is missing**, so it isn't configured as a trunk, and VLAN traffic toward Server 1 can't cross it.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. What is the cause of the error that is displayed in the configuration of inter-VLAN routing on router CiscoVille?

options.text: The gig0/0 interface does not support inter-VLAN routing.
The no shutdown command has not been configured.
The IP address on CiscoVille is incorrect.
The encapsulation dot1Q 20 command has not been configured.​

explain.s: On a router subinterface, you have to set the VLAN tag with **encapsulation dot1Q** *before* IOS accepts an IP address. That's why the error appears.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. A network administrator has configured router CiscoVille with the above commands to provide inter-VLAN routing. What command will be required on a switch that is connected to the Gi0/0 interface on router CiscoVille to allow inter-VLAN routing?​
questions.original: When they are configured for inter-VLAN routing, routers do not support the dynamic trunking protocol that is used by switches. For router-on-a-stick configurations to function, a connected switch must use the command switchport mode trunk.

explain.s: Routers don't negotiate DTP, so the switch port facing a router-on-a-stick must be set as a trunk manually.
x: dynamic desirable relies on DTP replies, which the router never sends.

questions.question: A high school uses VLAN15 for the laboratory network and VLAN30 for the faculty network. What is required to enable communication between these two VLANs while using the router-on-a-stick approach?

options.text: A router with at least two LAN interfaces is needed.
Two groups of switches are needed, each with ports that are configured for one VLAN.
A switch with a port that is configured as a trunk is needed when connecting to the router.

questions.original: With router-on-a-stick, inter-VLAN routing is performed by a router with a single router interface that is connected to a switch port configured with trunk mode. Multiple subinterfaces, each configured for a VLAN, can be configured under the single physical router interface. Switches can have ports that are assigned to different VLANs, but communication between those VLANs requires routing function from the router. A multilayer switch is not used in a router-on-a-stick approach to inter-VLAN routing.

explain.s: Router-on-a-stick uses **one router interface split into subinterfaces**, one per VLAN. That requires the switch port connecting to the router to be a **trunk**.
x: A multilayer switch is a different method (SVIs).
Needing one router port per VLAN is the legacy method.

questions.question: When routing a large number of VLANs, what are two disadvantages of using the router-on-a-stick inter-VLAN routing method rather than the multilayer switch inter-VLAN routing method? (Choose two.)

options.text: Router-on-a-stick requires subinterfaces to be configured on the same subnets.
Router-on-a-stick requires multiple physical interfaces on a router.
Multiple subinterfaces may impact the traffic flow speed.

questions.original: With the router-on-a-stick inter-VLAN routing method, a dedicated router is required. It only needs one physical interface on the router to route traffic among multiple VLANs, by using subinterfaces on one physical interface. On the other hand, since traffic of all VLANs will have to go through the same physical interfaces, the throughput will be impacted. Also, a multilayer switch can use multiple SVIs to perform inter-VLAN routing.

explain.s: Router-on-a-stick needs a **dedicated router**, and all VLANs share **one physical link**. With many VLANs that link becomes a bottleneck. A multilayer switch routes in hardware between SVIs instead.
x: SVIs belong to the multilayer-switch method.

explain.s: `shutdown` **administratively disables** the interface you're configuring, whether it is physical or an SVI. `no shutdown` turns it back on.

The shutdown command is used in Cisco IOS to administratively disable or turn off a specific interface. This applies to both physical interfaces (such as interface FastEthernet 0/1) and virtual / logical interfaces (such as an SVI like interface VLAN 10).
When executed within the interface configuration mode (config-if), the interface immediately transitions to an “Administratively Down” state, completely halting all data traffic through it. To reverse this effect and re-enable the interface, the inverse command no shutdown must be used instead.

Consequently, when the technician executes this command within the interface configuration mode (config-if), they are configuring a logical/virtual interface, which successfully applies the global unicast IPv6 address to that specific SVI.

explain.s: On a 2960 the IPv6 address goes on the **SVI**, which is the switch's virtual management interface.

The Cisco IOS Command Line Interface (CLI) uses a strict hierarchical structure. When the prompt displays (config-if)#, it indicates that the technician is currently inside the interface configuration sub-mode.
Issuing the exit command moves the user back exactly one level in the command hierarchy. As a result, the switch leaves the interface sub-mode and returns to global configuration mode, changing the CLI prompt back to branchSW(config)#.

explain.s: `exit` goes **up one level**: from interface mode back to **global configuration mode**. (`end` or Ctrl+Z jumps straight to privileged EXEC mode.)

questions.question: A technician is configuring a new Cisco 2960 switch. What is the effect of issuing the BranchSw(config-if)# duplex full command?

questions.original:
The duplex full command configures the switch interface to operate in full-duplex mode, enabling simultaneous two-way communication. This means that both the switch port and the connected device can transmit and receive data at the exact same time without causing any network collisions.
In contrast, if the interface were configured with duplex half, data could only flow in one direction at a time, forcing devices to take turns transmitting and introducing the risk of collisions. Implementing Full-Duplex maximizes bandwidth efficiency and significantly improves network performance on the link.

explain.s: **Full duplex** means the port sends and receives **at the same time**, with no collisions. Half duplex sends in only one direction at a time.

questions.question: What type of VLAN should not carry voice and network management traffic?
questions.original: A data VLAN, also referred to as a user VLAN, is specifically designed to carry user-generated network traffic such as web browsing, emails, or file transfers. For both security and performance reasons, network design best practices dictate that a data VLAN should not carry high-priority voice traffic (VoIP) or critical network management traffic (such as SSH, Telnet, or SNMP). Separating these distinct types of traffic into dedicated VLANs ensures that regular user data congestion does not negatively impact essential network services or infrastructure management.

explain.s: A **data (user) VLAN** carries ordinary user traffic. Voice and management traffic should each have their own VLAN, for QoS and security.

questions.question: What type of VLAN is designed to reserve bandwidth to ensure IP Phone quality?
questions.original: A voice VLAN is specifically designed and configured to carry Voice over IP (VoIP) traffic from IP phones. Because voice communications are highly sensitive to network delay and jitter, a voice VLAN allows the implementation of Quality of Service (QoS) and traffic prioritization policies. This mechanism reserves the required network bandwidth to ensure crystal-clear and uninterrupted phone conversations by isolating critical voice streams from regular, lower-priority data traffic.

explain.s: A **voice VLAN** separates IP-phone traffic so QoS can prioritize it and give calls the bandwidth they need.

questions.question: What type of VLAN is initially the management VLAN?
questions.original: In the out-of-the-box factory configuration of a Cisco switch, the default VLAN (VLAN 1) serves multiple foundational roles: it is the default data VLAN, the default native VLAN, and also the initial management VLAN. This means that before any custom configuration is applied, the switch's virtual interface (interface vlan 1) is the active logical interface used to assign an IP address for remote management. However, due to security best practices, it is highly recommended to change the management VLAN to a unique, dedicated VLAN separate from VLAN 1.

explain.s: Out of the box, **VLAN 1, the default VLAN**, is also the native VLAN and the **management VLAN** (interface vlan 1). Best practice is to move management to a dedicated VLAN.

questions.question: What type of VLAN is designed to have a delay of less than 150 ms across the network?
questions.original: A voice VLAN is explicitly designed to carry Voice over IP (VoIP) traffic. Because real-time voice communications are highly sensitive to network delay and jitter, industry standards (including Cisco guidelines) state that the one-way target delay across the network should not exceed 150 ms. To satisfy this stringent requirement, switches segment voice streams into a dedicated VLAN where Quality of Service (QoS) policies can be enforced to prioritize voice packets over regular data traffic.

explain.s: Voice traffic needs low delay, so the target is **under 150 ms one way**. A **voice VLAN** with QoS helps meet it.

questions.question: What type of VLAN is used to separate the network into groups of users or devices?
questions.original: A data VLAN, also referred to as a user VLAN, is specifically designed and configured to carry user-generated network traffic (such as web browsing, emails, or file transfers). The primary purpose of a data VLAN is to separate the network into logical groups of users or devices based on their roles or functions. This practice ensures that regular user data traffic is isolated from critical network management traffic and high-priority voice (VoIP) traffic.

explain.s: **Data VLANs** split users and devices into logical groups, such as by department, each in its own broadcast domain.

questions.question: What type of VLAN is configured specifically for network traffic such as SSH, Telnet, HTTPS, HTTP, and SNMP?
questions.original: A management VLAN is any VLAN that is configured to provide remote management access to a switch. Network management traffic such as SSH, Telnet, HTTPS, HTTP, and SNMP is specifically assigned to this VLAN to ensure that IT personnel can securely configure, monitor, and troubleshoot network devices. This isolates critical infrastructure management traffic from regular user data traffic. By default, Cisco switches use VLAN 1 as the initial management VLAN, although security best practices dictate changing this to a unique, dedicated VLAN.

explain.s: The **management VLAN** carries traffic used to manage devices remotely: SSH, Telnet, HTTP/HTTPS and SNMP. The switch's management SVI lives in this VLAN.

questions.question: What type of VLAN supports untagged traffic?
questions.original: On a switched network utilizing the IEEE 802.1Q encapsulation standard for trunk links, all data frames are normally tagged with a specific VLAN ID to identify their network of origin. The only exception to this rule is the native VLAN. Traffic belonging to the native VLAN is transmitted across the trunk link completely untagged. When the switch on the receiving end of the trunk encounters an untagged frame, it automatically associates it with its locally configured native VLAN.

explain.s: On an 802.1Q trunk, frames in the **native VLAN** are sent **untagged**. A switch that receives an untagged frame puts it in its own native VLAN.

questions.question: What type of VLAN supports untagged traffic?
questions.original: On a switched network utilizing the IEEE 802.1Q encapsulation standard for trunk links, all data frames are normally tagged with a specific VLAN ID to identify their network of origin. The only exception to this rule is the native VLAN. Traffic belonging to the native VLAN is transmitted across the trunk link completely untagged. When the switch on the receiving end of the trunk encounters an untagged frame, it automatically associates it with its locally configured native VLAN.

explain.s: Only the **native VLAN** travels **untagged** across an 802.1Q trunk. Every other VLAN gets a tag.

questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. The network administrator wants to configure Switch1 to allow SSH connections and prohibit Telnet connections. How should the network administrator change the displayed configuration to satisfy the requirement?

Therefore, the network administrator needs to modify the transport input command to specify only ssh, forcing the switch to drop any Telnet connection attempts while keeping SSH active.

explain.s: `transport input all` allows both Telnet and SSH. To allow **SSH only**, change it on the VTY lines.

questions.question: Which type of VLAN is used to designate which traffic is untagged when crossing a trunk port?
questions.original: A native VLAN is the VLAN that does not receive a VLAN tag in the IEEE 802.1Q frame header. Cisco best practices recommend the use of an unused VLAN (not a data VLAN, the default VLAN of VLAN 1, or the management VLAN) as the native VLAN whenever possible.

questions.question: What type of VLAN is configured specifically for network traffic such as SSH, Telnet, HTTPS, HHTP, and SNMP?

questions.question: Which Layer 2 attack will result in legitimate users not getting valid IP addresses?
questions.original: The DHCP starvation attack causes the exhaustion of the IP address pool of a DHCP server before legitimate users can obtain valid IP addresses.

explain.s: In **DHCP starvation**, the attacker sends a flood of DHCPDISCOVERs from fake MAC addresses and **uses up every address in the pool**. Real users then can't get an IP address. Mitigate it with port security and DHCP snooping.

questions.question: What mitigation plan is best for thwarting a DoS attack that is creating a MAC address table overflow?

options.text: Place unused ports in an unused VLAN.

questions.original: A MAC address (CAM) table overflow attack, buffer overflow, and MAC address spoofing can all be mitigated by configuring port security. Placing unused ports in an unused VLAN prevents unauthorized wired connectivity.

explain.s: A MAC (CAM) table overflow happens when one port sends thousands of fake source MACs. **Port security** caps how many MACs a port can learn, which stops it.
x: Disabling DTP stops VLAN hopping.
Disabling STP would allow loops.
